draft.text:
Optical Diffractive Neural Networks (ODNNs) have emerged as a distinct computational paradigm, fundamentally replacing electronic weight matrices with spatially varying phase profiles to implement linear transformations via diffraction. This review synthesizes current research to evaluate ODNNs not merely as optical accelerators, but as unique physical computers where wave physics dictates computational expressivity. By leveraging the inherent parallelism of light, these systems offer ultra-low latency and exceptional energy efficiency for specific inference tasks, effectively addressing the von Neumann bottleneck associated with conventional electronic architectures. However, this review argues that such advantages are currently domain-specific; ODNNs excel in throughput for pre-defined linear operations but do not yet constitute a general-purpose replacement for electronic processors due to fundamental physical constraints.

We systematically examine the critical tensions limiting widespread deployment, specifically the "nonlinearity bottleneck" inherent in passive diffractive layers and the persistent "simulation-to-reality" gap caused by fabrication tolerances and material dispersion. The analysis covers diverse training paradigms, including physics-aware algorithms and hardware-in-the-loop optimization, alongside a comparative assessment of static versus reconfigurable hardware platforms. While applications in imaging and pattern recognition have transitioned from theory to functional prototypes, their maturity varies significantly, with many systems remaining vulnerable to environmental perturbations. Consequently, the field appears to be shifting away from pursuing entirely all-optical general-purpose computers. Instead, the most viable trajectory involves hybrid electro-optical co-design, which combines the speed of diffractive layers for linear feature extraction with the flexibility of electronic components for nonlinearity and error correction. Future progress depends on establishing standardized benchmarks and robust training protocols that embed manufacturing constraints, ensuring a transition from fragile laboratory demonstrations to scalable, resilient optical artificial intelligence.
